title: Mini-bucket smoothing and kernel affinity draft
content:
Summary:
This is an exploratory design note for a lightweight "mini-bucket" scheduling layer combined with kernel affinity scoring and a KV-cache compatibility contract. Goal: reduce wasted padding tokens across a mixed-length workload while keeping scheduling overhead low and preserving fast, kernel-optimized execution paths.

Context / motivation:
- We frequently see long-tailed sequence length distributions: lots of short completions (10-40 tokens) plus spikes of long context generation (>1k tokens). Current coarse-grained bucketing (power-of-two or wide bins) either wastes tokens (padding short requests to large bins) or fragments GPU utilization (too many tiny groups).
- Advanced packing and prefix-clustering help, but introduce scheduling latency and complexity when combined with kernel variants that expect particular sequence shapes (e.g., fused attention kernels vs. block-sparse kernels).
- KV cache reuse across requests is critical for cost, but different kernel backends prefer different KV memory layouts. We need an approach that balances padding waste, kernel efficiency, and KV reuse.

Design principles:
- Keep per-request scheduling decisions O(1) and cheap to compute on the edge path.
- Favor policies that are robust to bursty arrivals and unpredictable length labels.
- Allow soft affinity to kernels: routing should prefer an efficient kernel but can fall back when deadlines require.
- Maintain a minimal compatibility contract for KV cache so that cached prefixes can be reused across kernel variants or converted cheaply.

Core idea: Mini-buckets + smoothing
- Mini-buckets: small, dense buckets representing narrow sequence-length ranges. Example bucket sizes: 8, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128. These are intentionally fine-grained for short/medium sequences and then coarser for long ones.
- Smoothing: a short request is allowed to wait up to a small, config-driven delay delta (e.g., 3-15ms) to be grouped with other similar-length requests; if it waits beyond delta or is close to deadline, it is scheduled early and optionally sent to a fast fallback kernel.
- Mini-buckets reduce the amount of zero-padding for short requests and increase the probability that when packed, the batch will match a kernel's optimized input shape.

Kernel affinity scoring (soft):
For each (bucket, kernel) pair compute a lightweight affinity score that combines:
1) kernel_efficiency: offline/profiled tokens/sec or latency per-token for the canonical shape.
2) wait_penalty: how long the head request in that bucket would need to wait to reach a reasonable batch size.
3) kv_cost: estimated cost to materialize or translate KV cache to the kernel's expected layout (0 for native layout, small constant for in-place, larger for reformat).
Affinity = alpha * kernel_efficiency - beta * wait_penalty - gamma * kv_cost (normalized).
- alpha/beta/gamma are tuned per-cluster and can be dynamic (e.g., during overload increase beta to penalize waiting).
- Scheduling selects the kernel with highest affinity that is compatible with the request's deadline. If affinity gaps are small, prefer the kernel with higher KV reuse to reduce end-to-end cost.

KV compatibility contract (minimal):
- Canonical prefix hash: every request computes a small deterministic prefix hash of the token IDs (first N tokens or last token boundary) that can be used to look up cached KV blocks.
- Layout tags: when we materialize KV for a request we tag it with a small string indicating layout variant (e.g., kv-row-major, kv-chunked-16, kv-quant8).
- Convert-on-demand: if a kernel requires a different layout, we allow a single-pass conversion routine that has predictable latency; conversions are charged to a budget to avoid excessive reformat costs.
- Shared prefixes across buckets: mini-buckets must not break KV sharing. When two requests share canonical prefix hash, scheduler will prefer to collocate them onto a worker that already has the KV materialized for one of the kernel variants.

Graceful truncation and deadline-aware falling back
- When a request is close to its client deadline and the expected wait to form a mini-bucket would exceed the slack, we can: (a) send the request immediately to a fast but slightly less efficient kernel (fast-fallback), or (b) perform a local truncation heuristic for generation requests where partial generations are acceptable (truncate-to-last-sentence or to token budget).
- Fast-fallback kernels are pre-warmed worker lanes with conservative memory layouts and small batch focus; they return lower throughput but maintain low tail latency.

KV eviction + hot-prefix tracking
- Maintain a per-worker hot-prefix LRU with time-decay weighting that prefers prefixes that hit on recent requests.
- When memory pressure requires eviction, evict less popular prefixes even if they are large; provide a lightweight prefetcher that can pull back evicted KV when a collocated request is scheduled.
- Track prefix co-occurrence graphs to opportunistically pre-materialize small shared prefixes for expected traffic (use simple frequency-based heuristics, no graph learning in first iteration).

Simulation and metrics to validate
- Offline simulator that takes real traffic traces (from hosted API) and runs: current baseline packing, coarse buckets, and mini-buckets with smoothing. Measure: padded_tokens_per_request, avg_latency, p95_latency, token_cost_per_model_token (estimate by kernel profile + padding).
- Metrics to observe in-canary: wasted_padding_rate, kv_reuse_rate, per-kernel-utilization, request_wait_histogram, p50/p95/p99 latency, tail-failure rate.

Compatibility and rollout plan
- Phase 0: Implement simulator + profiler for kernel efficiency and KV conversion cost. 2 weeks.
- Phase 1: Canary mini-buckets + no-kv-affinity (i.e., affinity uses only efficiency and wait). Small % of traffic, compare to current. 3 weeks.
- Phase 2: Introduce KV affinity and canonical prefix hashing, enable local collocation preference. Expand canary. 4 weeks.
- Phase 3: Enable graceful truncation and fast-fallback lanes; tune alpha/beta/gamma automatically based on utilization signals. 4 weeks.

Open questions / risks:
- How to pick bucket boundaries automatically? We can start from quantiles of historical length distribution per-model, but multi-tenant variance complicates this.
- Cost of KV conversion: will conversions dominate gains for workloads with heavily mixed kernels? Need accurate profiling.
- Does fine-grained bucketing increase scheduling overhead? We believe our O(1) bucket index and short wait delta keeps overhead low, but need load testing.
- Long sequences: mini-buckets are most effective for short/medium lengths — need strategy for tails (use coarser bins or stream-mode with streaming kernels).

Implementation notes / checklist:
- lightweight bucket index function (token_len -> bucket_id) + per-bucket queue with atomic counters
- affinity scorer module with runtime-configurable weights and per-kernel profiles
- canonical prefix hasher + small on-disk index for hot prefixes per worker
- KV layout tags + conversion helpers in runtime library (C++)
- fallbacks: a pre-warmed lane on each worker for small-batch low-latency handling
- telemetry hooks: log chosen bucket, kernel, kv_layout_tag, wait_time, padding_waste_per_request

To do next (short term):
- Miguel: build offline simulator and ingest last 30 days of hosted-api traces (ticket assigned).
- Rina: add microbenchmarks for KV conversion routines across our kernels; measure latency and extra memory.
- Ethan: prototype bucket index + per-bucket atomic counters in the scheduler; simulate small wait deltas.
- Aisha: coordinate canary plan and draft rollout gating criteria (SLO delta, cost delta).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: avoid heavy global packing control in the first iteration. We trade some global optimality for fast iteration and predictable per-worker behavior.
- Please flag any missing attacker surface for KV materialization or potential for noisy neighbor effects when collocating prefixes.

-- end --
